title: The Body at the Negotiation Table
hook: Negotiators are taught to hunt for tells, but the body's real power at the table lies in what it does to trust, patience and your own judgment.
why:
Negotiation attracts more body language folklore than almost any other setting. Books and courses promise to teach you to spot a bluff from a touch of the nose, to dominate the room with your posture, to mirror your counterpart into agreement and to use anger to extract concessions. Men in particular are often taught that negotiation is a contest of nerve, won by the one who gives least away and reads the other best.

The research tells a different story. The tells are mostly unreliable, as the chapter on deception in Part I showed. What the body does reliably at the table is quieter: it builds or erodes trust, it carries emotions that change what the other side concedes, and it shapes your own judgment through fatigue and arousal. This chapter covers the myth of the tell, mimicry and why the honest version of it works better, what anger does and when it backfires, why faked emotion costs trust, when seeing each other helps, and how to manage your own body through a long negotiation. Throughout, it holds to the line this book draws: understanding these effects is for negotiating better and more honestly, not for manipulating the person across the table.

teach.p:
The idea of the tell comes from poker, where a player's unconscious habit, such as a twitch when bluffing, might give away the strength of a hand. Negotiation books borrowed the idea and multiplied it: a hand to the nose means a lie, crossed arms mean resistance, a glance to the side means the price has room to move. Negotiators are encouraged to watch for these signs and to act on them.

The evidence does not support this. As the chapter on deception in Part I described, people's accuracy at detecting lies from behaviour is only slightly better than chance, and the behaviours most often believed to signal lying, such as averted gaze and fidgeting, are among the weakest cues. There is no reason to think negotiators are better at this than anyone else, and some reason to think they are worse, because the stakes make them more suspicious.

Acting on false tells is costly. A negotiator who decides that his counterpart is bluffing because she touched her face may push too hard, lose a deal that was available, or damage a relationship that mattered more than the deal. A negotiator convinced he can read the other side also tends to stop asking questions, because he believes he already knows the answers.

What can be read, with care, is the general state of a conversation: whether the other side seems engaged or withdrawn, tense or at ease, more or less willing to keep talking. These readings are useful as prompts to ask, not as verdicts. The figure here sits with a hand to his face, a gesture a negotiation book might call a sign of doubt or deceit. It is far more likely that he is thinking.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if specific behaviours such as touching the face reliably revealed bluffs in negotiation. Research on deception finds that such cues are weak and that people's accuracy at detecting lies is only slightly above chance.

teach.p:
One body language effect does have good evidence at the table. In 2008 William Maddux, Elizabeth Mullen and Adam Galinsky asked some negotiators to subtly mimic their counterparts' posture and mannerisms: if the other person leaned back, they would lean back a little later; if the other touched their face, they would do something similar after a pause. Other negotiators were told not to mimic.

Negotiators who mimicked achieved better outcomes for themselves and for the pair. In a negotiation where a deal could only be reached by uncovering the parties' underlying interests, mimickers were much more likely to reach agreement. The researchers found that the effect worked through trust: counterparts who were mimicked trusted the mimicker more, and so shared more information about what they really needed.

This fits a wider body of research. Part VI described the chameleon effect: people unconsciously mimic those they interact with, and being mimicked tends to increase liking. Mimicry seems to work as a signal that two people are in tune, and trust follows.

Two cautions follow. First, the negotiators in the study were told to mimic subtly, with a delay. Most people find it unsettling to realise they are being copied, and an obviously mirrored gesture reads as a technique rather than as rapport. Second, and more important, there is a question about whether deliberate mimicry is something you should do at all, which the next block takes up. The figures here sit across a table from each other, the classic arrangement of a negotiation. How they sit in relation to each other will shape how much they trust each other, whether or not either of them is thinking about it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if negotiators who mimicked their counterparts reached deals no more often than those who did not. In Maddux and colleagues' study they reached more deals, through greater trust, though the mimicry was deliberately subtle.

teach.p:
Deliberately mimicking someone to make them trust you is, on any honest reading, a way of manufacturing a signal. You are producing the appearance of being in tune in order to obtain information the other person might not otherwise share. This book does not teach techniques of that kind, and the reason is practical as well as ethical: a negotiation is usually one meeting in a longer relationship, and trust obtained by technique is fragile when it is discovered.

There is a better route to the same place. Natural mimicry is not something people decide to do. It arises when two people are genuinely attending to each other. If you listen closely to your counterpart, are curious about what they need, and are actually trying to find an agreement that works for both of you, your bodies will tend to fall into step without any instruction. The trust that follows is real, because the attention behind it is real.

In practice this means spending the energy you might have spent watching for tells or copying gestures on understanding the other side. Ask what matters to them and why. Reflect back what you heard, in your own words. Notice when they seem to relax or tighten, and ask about it rather than drawing conclusions. Let silence sit after a question, rather than filling it with your own argument.

This is slower than a trick, and it does not guarantee a better deal on any single occasion. But it builds the kind of trust that survives the end of the negotiation and makes the next one easier. The figure here listens with attention, the posture from which honest rapport grows. The study's effect was carried by trust. Earning it is better than engineering it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if genuine attention produced no rapport or trust without deliberate mimicry. Research on natural mimicry suggests the opposite: people fall into step when they are genuinely engaged with each other.
teach.pullQuote: The mimicry study's effect was carried by trust. Earning it is better than engineering it.

teach.h: What anger does at the table.
teach.p:
Emotion travels across a negotiating table, and anger has been studied more than any other. In 2004 Gerben van Kleef, Carsten de Dreu and Antony Manstead had people negotiate over the sale of mobile phones with a counterpart who, through scripted messages, appeared either angry or happy. People conceded more to the angry counterpart than to the happy one.

The reason was inference. People used the counterpart's anger as information about his limits: if he was angry at the offer, he must be close to walking away, so it was safer to concede. When the angry counterpart had already made large concessions himself, the effect disappeared, because his anger no longer suggested he was near his limit. Later work by the same team found that the effect was strongest for people with little power. Negotiators with strong alternatives were largely unmoved by the other side's anger.

It would be easy to conclude that anger is a useful tactic. The next block explains why that conclusion is too quick. For now, the useful lesson is about reading. When your counterpart shows anger, it may be telling you something true about their limits, or it may not. Treat it as a question rather than an answer: ask what specifically is unacceptable to them and why.

It is also worth noticing what anger does to you. Facing an angry counterpart, most people feel pressure to make the discomfort stop, and conceding is the quickest way. Naming that pressure to yourself, and taking a breath or a break before responding, gives you the chance to decide rather than react. The figure here raises his chin, a small sign of challenge. How much it moves you depends partly on how much power you have and how badly you need the deal.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if negotiators conceded no more to an angry counterpart than to a happy one. In Van Kleef and colleagues' study they conceded more, because they read anger as a sign that the other side was near its limit.

teach.p:
Anger's effect at the table turns out to depend heavily on context. In 2010 Hajo Adam, Aiwa Shirako and William Maddux found that expressing anger drew larger concessions from European American negotiators but smaller concessions from Asian and Asian American negotiators. When the researchers told participants that anger was an acceptable part of negotiating, the cultural difference largely disappeared. When they told them it was unacceptable, anger backfired for everyone. What mattered was whether anger was seen as appropriate.

Whether the anger is real matters too. In 2013 Stéphane Côté, Ivona Hideg and Gerben van Kleef compared anger that a negotiator actually felt with anger that was put on for show. Faked anger, displayed without being felt, made counterparts demand more, not less, because it reduced their trust. Felt anger lowered demands, because the person seemed tough. People often sense the difference between felt and performed emotion, even when they cannot say how.

Together, these findings undercut the idea of anger as a tactic. Performed anger tends to cost trust and can raise the other side's demands. Even real anger helps only where the other side sees it as legitimate, and the person who uses it pays a price in the relationship.

If you are genuinely angry in a negotiation, the honest course is to say what you are angry about and why, in words, rather than letting it leak out as pressure or performing more of it than you feel. If you are not angry, do not pretend. The figure here stands with arms crossed tightly, a posture that can look like resolve or like barely contained anger. Which it reads as, and what it costs, depends on whether it is real and whether the room accepts it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if faked anger extracted concessions as well as felt anger. Côté and colleagues found that faked anger raised counterparts' demands by reducing their trust, while felt anger lowered them.
teach.pullQuote: Performed anger costs trust. If you are angry, say what about, in words; if you are not, do not pretend.

teach.p:
Many negotiations now happen by email, on the phone or over video rather than face to face. Does it matter whether the parties can see each other? In 2012 Roderick Swaab, Adam Galinsky, Victoria Medvec and Daniel Diermeier combined the results of many studies of negotiation and group decisions to find out.

Their answer was that it depends on what the parties bring to the table. For people who started out neutral towards each other, with no particular relationship, richer channels such as video and face-to-face meetings led to better outcomes than text. For people already inclined to cooperate, the channel made little difference. For people who were already hostile, richer channels could make outcomes worse, perhaps because seeing and hearing each other gave more opportunity to provoke and react.

The researchers also found that the benefit of rich channels for neutral parties was weaker in East Asian cultures than in Western ones, a reminder that none of these findings applies everywhere.

This gives a practical rule of thumb. When you are negotiating with a stranger, try to meet in person or at least by video for the early stages, where trust is built and interests are explored. When a relationship has turned hostile, it may help to cool things with written exchanges, a mediator or a break before meeting again. And on video, the lessons from the earlier chapters of this part apply: a camera at eye level, a well-lit face and an attentive posture all carry more weight than in a room. The figure here is on a video call, the setting where many negotiations now begin.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if seeing each other made no difference to negotiations between strangers. Swaab and colleagues found that richer channels improved outcomes for neutral parties, though not for those already cooperative or hostile.

teach.h: Your own body at the table.
teach.p:
The body that matters most in a negotiation is often your own. Long negotiations are physically demanding. Hours of concentration, little food, poor sleep before an important meeting and the steady arousal of a high-stakes exchange all affect judgment. Part II's chapters on stress and sleep looked at how depletion wears down mood, patience and judgment. At the table, that often shows up as conceding late in the day simply to be finished, or digging in over something small out of irritation.

A few practices help. Eat beforehand and keep water nearby. Schedule breaks into long sessions, and take one before any significant decision rather than after. Notice your own signs of arousal, such as a tight jaw, shallow breathing or a rising voice, and treat them as a signal to slow down. When you feel pressure to agree immediately, it is almost always acceptable to say that you need a short time to think.

Changing the physical arrangement can help too. Part III described the side-by-side principle: men often talk more easily when they are not face to face. Some negotiators find that a walk together, or sitting side by side in front of a whiteboard or a shared document, turns a contest into a joint problem. The table that separates two parties also defines them as opponents, and moving away from it can change that.

None of this guarantees a good deal. It protects the quality of your own thinking, which is the one thing at the table you can fully control. The figures here walk side by side, turned slightly towards each other. A difficult conversation is often easier to have in motion, looking at the same path rather than at each other.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if fatigue, hunger and stress had no effect on negotiators' decisions. Research on stress and sleep loss, discussed in Part II, suggests they impair judgment and emotional control, which is why breaks protect decisions.

caseStudy:
Marcus, thirty-six, is a procurement manager negotiating the renewal of a large contract with a software supplier. Before the first meeting he read a book on negotiation body language. He went in watching for tells, mirroring the account manager's posture, and planning to show anger at the first price to signal that it was unacceptable.

It went badly. He thought the account manager touched her face when she named the price and decided she was bluffing, so he pushed hard. His show of anger felt false even to him, and she became guarded and stopped volunteering information. The meeting ended with both sides further apart than when they started.

Before the second meeting, a more experienced colleague asked him what the supplier actually needed from the deal. Marcus did not know. He had spent the first meeting watching her hands instead of asking.

This time he suggested they work through the contract side by side, on a shared screen. He asked about her company's constraints and listened. It turned out that her company cared far more about a longer contract term than about the headline price, and that Marcus's company could easily commit to three years. They found an agreement that cut the price and extended the term. When a point about support hours frustrated him, he said plainly that it was a problem for his team and why, rather than performing anger. He took a break before agreeing to the final terms, though he was fairly sure of them.

Afterwards he reflected that he had read nothing useful from her body in either meeting. What had changed the outcome was that, the second time, he had been paying attention to her rather than watching her.
observe: Notice, in your next negotiation or difficult conversation, whether you are watching for signs or listening for needs.
Notice whether you and the other person fall into similar postures as the conversation goes on, without either of you deciding to.
Notice how you respond when someone across the table shows anger, and whether you feel pressure to concede.
Notice your own physical state late in a long meeting, and whether it is affecting what you are willing to agree to.

drills.name: Interests Not Tells
steps: Before your next negotiation, large or small, write down what you think the other side needs and why.
Write three open questions that would help you find out, such as what matters most to you here.
In the conversation, ask them and listen, rather than watching for signs of bluffing.
Afterwards, note what you learned that you could not have read from their body.
Compare your notes with what you assumed beforehand.
variations: Before a small everyday negotiation, such as with a tradesperson or a seller online, write three questions about what the other person needs, and ask them.
After a negotiation, write down any moment when you were tempted to read a tell, and what you would have concluded from it.
Ask a colleague who negotiates often what they wish they had asked in their last deal, and add it to your list of questions.

drills.name: Name the Pressure
steps: In your next tense conversation, notice the moment you feel pressure to agree or give way.
Name it silently: I am feeling pressure to end this.
Take one slow breath before responding.
If the decision matters, say you need a short time to think.
Afterwards, note whether pausing changed what you decided.
variations: Practise holding a silence of four or five seconds after a question in an ordinary conversation, and notice how the other person fills it.
Write down, after a tense conversation, the exact moment you felt the most pressure to agree, and what you would do differently there.
Agree a word with a colleague negotiating alongside you that means "let's take a break", and use it once.

drills.name: Words for Anger
steps: Think of a point in a past negotiation or argument where you felt angry.
Write one or two sentences that say what you were angry about and why, without blame or threat.
Practise saying them aloud, in an even voice.
Next time you feel anger in a negotiation, use words like these rather than letting it leak as pressure.
variations: Write your sentence about anger for a situation at home, such as a dispute with a neighbour, as well as one at work.
Practise saying your sentence to a friend who interrupts you angrily, keeping your voice even, and notice what happens to theirs.
Notice, in your next disagreement, whether the other person's anger drops when you put your own frustration into calm words.

drills.name: Change the Geometry
steps: Choose a negotiation or difficult conversation coming up.
Plan to hold part of it side by side, over a shared document, whiteboard or walk.
Notice whether the conversation feels more or less adversarial than across a table.
Ask the other person afterwards how it felt to them.
Decide whether to use the arrangement again.
variations: Try working through a shared document side by side on a video call, with one person sharing the screen, and notice whether it feels less like a contest.
For a conversation that has already turned hostile, try exchanging written proposals first and meeting only once the gap has narrowed.
In a meeting where you usually sit across from the other side, put the key figures on a screen at the end of the table, so that everyone faces them.

quiz.q: A negotiation coach claims that experienced negotiators can spot a bluff from tells such as touching the nose. What does the evidence suggest?
options: Experienced negotiators can spot bluffs reliably once they have learned the main tells
Lie detection from behaviour is barely above chance, and cues like face touching are weak
Face touching is a reliable sign of lying, but only when the stakes are very high
Bluffing can be detected from posture, though not from any gestures of the hands
quiz.explain: People detect lies from behaviour at only slightly better than chance, and the cues most often believed to reveal lying are among the weakest. Acting on false tells can cost a deal or a relationship.

quiz.q: In Maddux and colleagues' study, how did subtle mimicry help negotiators?
options: It made counterparts afraid of the mimicker, so they conceded more quickly
It distracted counterparts, so they did not notice the weakness of the offers
It increased trust, so counterparts shared more about what they really needed
It had no effect on outcomes, though it made the meetings feel more pleasant
quiz.explain: Mimicked counterparts trusted the mimicker more and shared more information, which made deals more likely. The mimicry was deliberately subtle; this book's view is that genuine attention is the honest route to the same trust.

quiz.q: Why did people concede more to an angry counterpart in Van Kleef and colleagues' study?
options: They read the anger as a sign the counterpart was close to walking away
They wanted to punish the counterpart for being rude by ending quickly
They believed angry people were more honest about their best offers
They found anger frightening, whatever the counterpart had already offered
quiz.explain: People used the anger as information about the other side's limits. When the angry counterpart had already conceded a lot, the effect disappeared.

quiz.q: What did Adam, Shirako and Maddux find about anger in negotiations across cultures?
options: Anger drew larger concessions from every group, though the effect was smaller for some
Anger backfired with every group, so it should never be used in any negotiation
Anger had no effect in any culture once the size of the offer was accounted for
Anger drew larger concessions from European Americans but smaller ones from Asian Americans
quiz.explain: The difference depended on whether anger was seen as appropriate. When participants were told anger was acceptable, it helped regardless of background; when told it was unacceptable, it backfired for everyone.

quiz.q: A colleague suggests you act angry at the supplier's first offer, even though you are not, to push the price down. What does the research suggest?
options: It will work well, because the supplier will read your anger as a sign of your limits
Faked anger tends to reduce trust and can lead the other side to demand more, not less
It will have no effect, because suppliers are trained to ignore emotion in negotiations
It works only if you keep it up for the whole negotiation without letting it slip at all
quiz.explain: Côté and colleagues found that faked anger raised counterparts' demands by reducing trust. Felt anger worked differently, but performing emotion you do not feel tends to backfire.

quiz.q: You are about to negotiate for the first time with a company you have never worked with. Which approach fits the research best?
options: Hold the early stages by video or in person, where trust can be built
Keep everything in email, so that you can control exactly what they see
Meet in person, but keep your face blank so they can read nothing at all
Send a lawyer to the first meeting, so that you are never seen in person
quiz.explain: For parties who start out neutral, richer channels such as video and face-to-face meetings tend to improve outcomes. Swaab and colleagues found the benefit did not hold for parties who were already hostile.

quiz.q: In Swaab and colleagues' analysis, what did richer channels such as video do for negotiators who were already hostile?
options: They could make outcomes worse, perhaps by giving more to provoke and react to
They always led to better outcomes, since faces and voices build trust between any two people
They made no difference, since hostile negotiators never reach any agreement at all
They helped only when the negotiators were from East Asian cultures, not elsewhere in the world
quiz.explain: For neutral parties, richer channels helped; for cooperative ones they made little difference; for hostile ones they could make things worse. Seeing and hearing each other gave more opportunity to provoke and react.

quiz.q: A client rings, angry, about an invoice, and threatens to cancel the whole order. What fits this chapter best?
options: Offer a large discount at once, since anger shows he is very close to walking away for good
Ask calmly what has changed for him and explain the invoice before offering anything
Match his anger, since showing toughness will make him respect you and back down quickly
Hang up immediately, since an angry customer will not listen to any explanation you give
quiz.explain: Anger is information about the person's situation, not proof of their limits. Finding out what has happened often shows that no concession is needed, or which one is.

quiz.q: Someone says anger always works in negotiation, because people concede to angry counterparts. What did van Kleef and colleagues' work show?
options: That the effect faded when the angry side had already conceded a lot, and was weak for those with strong alternatives
That anger works equally well on everyone, regardless of power or the alternatives they have available to them at the time
That anger always backfires, because every negotiator reads it as weakness and pushes harder against the angry person
That anger works only when it is faked, since genuine anger tends to frighten the other side away from the table entirely
quiz.explain: People conceded because they read anger as a sign of the other side's limits. When the angry counterpart had already made large concessions, or the negotiator had strong alternatives, the effect largely disappeared.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific negotiation or difficult conversation from the past year: over pay, a price, a deadline, a family decision. What were you watching for in the other person's body, and what did you conclude from it? Did you learn what they actually needed, and how? Describe one moment when emotion, theirs or yours, changed what happened. If you could go back, what would you do differently with your attention, your words or your own body?
reflection.guidance: Many people go into negotiations braced for a contest and come out having learned little about the other side. Be honest about whether you were reading or asking. Be specific about the moment emotion entered, and about whether anyone's emotion was real or performed.

failureMode: The first failure is to believe you can read bluffs from tells, and to push too hard on the strength of a touched nose or crossed arms. The second is to copy your counterpart's gestures as a technique, which is manipulative and often noticed, when genuine attention builds the same trust honestly. The third is to perform anger as a tactic, when faked anger tends to raise the other side's demands and cost trust. The fourth is to concede to an angry counterpart simply to make the discomfort stop, without asking what their anger is about. The fifth is to negotiate tired, hungry or rushed, and agree late in the day to things you would have refused in the morning. And the sixth is to treat the person across the table as an opponent to be read rather than a person to be understood.

moreCases.title: The buyer who found a tell
moreCases.scene:
Jen, thirty-four, is buying a used family car from a dealership on the edge of town. She has done her homework on prices and she has read a popular book on negotiation body language. When the salesman, Kev, names the price, she watches him closely. He glances to the side and touches his ear as he says the number. The book says that a glance away and a touch to the face mean a lie or room to move. Jen decides the price is padded.

She offers fifteen hundred pounds less. Kev says that he cannot do that, and that the price is already sharp. Jen, sure that she has seen through him, sits back, folds her arms and says she will walk. Kev comes down a hundred pounds, which Jen takes as confirmation that there is more. She holds out for another thousand. He apologises and says he cannot. She walks.

Over the next fortnight, she looks at four more cars of the same model and age. Three are priced higher than Kev's. The fourth is cheaper but has done twice the mileage. When she rings the first dealership again, the car has been sold.

Her brother, who sold cars for six years, tells her that Kev's figure was a fair one, and asks what she found out about the deal besides the price. Jen realises she had not asked about anything else.

She also noticed, she thought, that Kev's feet were pointing towards the door, which the book said meant he wanted to end the conversation. In fact the door was where the coffee machine was.

Kev, for his part, thought Jen was a serious buyer who had made up her mind not to trust him, and decided it was not worth offering her the extras he would usually have thrown in.
moreCases.misread:
Jen read a sideways glance and a touch to the ear as a sign that the price was padded, and pushed hard on the strength of it. She read Kev's small concession as proof that there was much more to come, when it was close to his limit.

And she read her own folded arms and threat to walk as strength, when they mostly told Kev that she was not interested in any deal he could actually offer.

Kev's own reading of her, as someone who would never be satisfied, was just as wrong, and cost him a sale he would happily have made.
moreCases.betterRead:
As the chapter on deception in Part I described, people detect lies from behaviour only slightly better than chance, and face-touching and averted gaze are among the weakest cues. Kev may have been thinking, remembering the figure or simply scratching his ear. Acting on a false tell led Jen to push past a fair price and lose the car. The better reading would have put the energy into questions rather than watching: what was included, whether there was a warranty, what they would give for her old car, whether servicing or tyres could be part of the deal. Many dealers have more room on extras than on the headline price. When Jen bought her next car, she asked those questions, got a year's servicing and new tyres included, and paid close to the asking price without feeling she had lost.

She also took a friend with her, to give her someone to think aloud with before agreeing.

moreCases.title: The silence after the number
moreCases.scene:
Omar, twenty-nine, has been a software tester for three years and has been doing a senior tester's job for the last eight months without the title or the pay. He has researched salaries and decided to ask his manager, Linda, for a rise of five thousand pounds. He has rehearsed the conversation in the shower all week.

In the meeting, he sets out his case, then names the figure. Linda looks at him, says nothing, and writes something on her pad. Her face is still. The silence lasts perhaps four seconds. To Omar it feels like a minute. He reads her stillness as a refusal, and before she has spoken, he says, "Or even three thousand would be great, I know budgets are tight." Linda looks up and says she will see what she can do.

Afterwards, he is furious with himself. He had decided in advance that five was the right number, and he had bargained himself down in four seconds, without Linda saying a word.

Three weeks later, Linda tells him that she has secured a rise of three thousand. She mentions, in passing, that she had written "5k, fair" on her pad during the meeting, and had been about to say she would push for it before he came in with the lower figure.

Omar had also read, the night before, that you should never be the first to name a number. He had named it first anyway, because Linda had asked him what he had in mind, and he had felt he could not refuse.
moreCases.misread:
Omar read Linda's silence and still face as a refusal, and lowered his own figure to escape the discomfort. Linda's silence had been her thinking, and her still face the ordinary face of someone writing a note.

He also read his own discomfort as information about Linda's answer, when it was information about how much he wanted the rise.

Linda, for her part, read his quick lower figure as a sign that he had overreached and knew it, which made the lower figure easier to settle on.
moreCases.betterRead:
In a negotiation, a silence after a number feels like pressure to the person who named it, and many people fill it with a concession, which amounts to negotiating against themselves. The pressure is real, but it is mostly inside the person feeling it. Linda's stillness was not a tell; as the chapter on the poker face earlier in this part described, a still face is easily read as disapproval when it may mean nothing of the kind. Omar's better approach, which he used at his next review, was to name the pressure to himself, breathe out slowly and wait. If the silence went on, he could ask a question: "How does that sound to you?" He practised holding a pause with a friend. At his next review, he named a figure, waited through Linda's silence, and got it.

He also learned to prepare a question to ask if the silence went on, so that he had something to say other than a lower figure.

moreCases.title: The father of the bride
moreCases.scene:
Bella, forty-five, runs a small florist's shop and does flowers for weddings. Three weeks before a large wedding, the bride's father, Keith, rings her about the final invoice, which is higher than the original quote because the couple added flowers for the church and two extra tables. He is angry. He says the invoice is outrageous, that he feels taken for a ride, and that he has a good mind to cancel the whole order. His voice is loud and he talks over her twice.

Bella hates conflict. Within two minutes she offers him twenty per cent off the invoice, which wipes out her profit on the job. Keith accepts, grudgingly, and rings off.

That evening, going through her emails, Bella finds the message from the bride confirming the extra flowers and the revised price, sent a month earlier. It occurs to her that Keith may never have seen it.

The next day the bride rings, embarrassed. Her father had been ill and had not been told about the changes, and had seen the invoice in the post with no explanation. She says that he is mortified and would like to pay the full amount. Bella says she will think about it, and puts the phone down feeling that she has learned something expensive.

She has given discounts before, to stop people being angry with her. She has never worked out what they cost her over a year, and she does not want to.

Keith had also said, near the end of the call, that he was "not made of money, whatever people think". Bella had heard it as a negotiating line. Later she wondered whether it had been the most important thing he said.
moreCases.misread:
Bella read Keith's anger as a sign that he was close to cancelling and that only a large concession would save the order. She read her own discomfort as a reason to end the conversation as fast as possible.

She also read the speed of her own concession as kindness, when it was mostly a way of ending a conversation she found frightening.

And she missed the clue in what he said, that he was not made of money, which pointed to worry rather than tactics.
moreCases.betterRead:
Van Kleef and colleagues found that people concede more to an angry counterpart because they read anger as information about the other side's limits: if he is angry, he must be near walking away. But anger is information about the person's situation, and the first job is to find out what the situation is. Keith was not near his limit; he was confused and frightened by an unexplained bill while he was unwell. Bella's better response, which she now uses, is to slow the call down: to say, calmly, "I can hear this has come as a shock, can I take you through what changed?", and to explain before offering anything. If a concession is warranted, she makes it after she understands the problem, not to stop the discomfort. She let Keith pay the full amount, and he sent her a box of chocolates.

She also changed her invoices, so that any change to an order now comes with a short note explaining what changed and when it was agreed, which has stopped most angry calls before they start.

moreCases.title: The partners on the screen
moreCases.scene:
Harry, fifty-six, and Jonny, fifty-three, founded a joinery business together twenty years ago. They have fallen out badly over the direction of the firm, and have agreed to split it: Jonny will buy Harry's share. They are no longer speaking except through their accountants. To save time, the accountants suggest that the four of them meet on a video call to agree the valuation.

The call goes wrong within ten minutes. Each partner can see the other's face in a small square, and each reads the worst into it. When Harry names his figure, he sees Jonny roll his eyes. When Jonny responds, Harry sees him smirk. Harry raises his voice; Jonny leans into his camera. Old grievances come up, about a contract in 2011 and a van that was never paid for. The accountants try to steer back to the figures, but the two men are now watching each other rather than the spreadsheet. The call ends with Harry leaving it.

Afterwards, Jonny's accountant, Seema, asks him whether he really smirked. Jonny says he was wincing at a figure, not smirking at Harry. Harry's accountant reports that Harry is now talking about lawyers.

Seema suggests a different approach. She has seen this before.

Both men had agreed beforehand that they would keep it professional. Both had prepared their figures carefully. Neither had prepared for the sight of the other man's face after six months of not seeing it.

Seema has worked on dozens of business separations, and she has noticed that the ones that go worst are often the ones where the partners still care most about what the other thinks of them.
moreCases.misread:
Each partner read the other's face on the screen as contempt: an eye-roll, a smirk, a lean into the camera. Each reacted to what he read, and the reactions confirmed the readings, until the valuation was lost in the history.

The accountants read the call as a failure of goodwill, when it was a failure of format: two hostile people given the richest possible view of each other's faces at the worst possible moment.

Jonny's wince and Harry's raised voice were both reactions to the figures and the history, not to each other's faces in the moment, but the faces were what each man saw.
moreCases.betterRead:
Swaab and colleagues found that richer channels such as video and face-to-face meetings helped negotiators who started out neutral, but could make things worse for people who were already hostile, perhaps because seeing each other gave more opportunity to provoke and react. Harry and Jonny were the second kind. Seema's better plan separated the two jobs. First, each side's proposals went back and forth in writing, through the accountants, where there were no faces to misread and time to think. When the gap had narrowed to a small sum, the four met in person at Seema's office, around a table with the spreadsheet on a screen at one end, so that everyone faced the numbers rather than each other. They agreed in an hour. Harry and Jonny shook hands at the end, briefly, which neither had expected.

Seema said afterwards that the most useful thing she had done was to keep their faces apart until the numbers were close, and then to give them a shared screen to look at instead of each other.

workedReading.title: Negotiating a job offer
workedReading.scene:
Leila, thirty-two, has been offered a job as a product manager at a larger company, and the recruiter, Tom, has rung to talk through the offer. The salary is below what she had hoped for, the start date is earlier than she can manage, and there is no mention of the flexible working she currently has. She likes the company and wants the job. She has never negotiated an offer before, and she is worried that asking for more will make them withdraw it. She asks Tom whether she can call him back in an hour, and he agrees. She spends the hour preparing, not by planning what to watch for in Tom's voice, but by working out what she needs and why, and what the company might need from her.

She has read that women who negotiate are sometimes judged harshly for it, and she is aware that the chapter on the glass ceiling places the problem in the evaluator. She decides that she will ask in a warm, plain way, and that if the company holds asking against her, that tells her something about the company.

steps.label: Prepare away from the table
steps.text:
She writes down her three priorities in order: flexible working two days a week, a start date six weeks out rather than three, and a salary five thousand higher. She notes her alternative, which is to stay where she is, reasonably happy. She writes three questions for Tom: what flexibility the team already has, why the start date matters to them, and how the salary was set. Knowing her alternative makes her less afraid of the conversation.

She also writes down what she can offer in return: flexibility on the start date if the salary moves, and a willingness to join a launch call before she starts. A negotiation goes better when both sides can see something to gain.

steps.label: Settle the body
steps.text:
Before she rings back, she stands up, walks around the flat once and takes two slow breaths with long exhales. She has noticed that her shoulders are up by her ears. She lets them drop. She puts a glass of water by the phone and her list in front of her. She decides to take the call standing, because her voice is steadier when she stands, and she wants it to sound like her ordinary voice.

She also turns off notifications on her laptop and closes the door, so that she will not be distracted mid-sentence by a message.

She also reminds herself that Tom wants to fill the role, and that a candidate who asks reasonable questions is usually seen as a serious one.

steps.label: Open warmly, then ask
steps.text:
She begins by telling Tom, truthfully, that she is pleased about the offer and excited about the role. Then she asks her questions before stating any demands. She learns that the team already works flexibly, that the start date is tied to a product launch, and that the salary was set at the bottom of a band. Each answer tells her something she could not have guessed, and none of it came from listening for tells.

She makes notes as Tom talks, and reads back what she has understood before moving on, which shows him that she has listened and catches one misunderstanding about the bonus.

steps.label: Leave room after the number
steps.text:
She says that she would like the salary to be five thousand higher, explains why in one sentence, and then stops. Tom is silent for a few seconds. She feels the pull to fill the silence with "but I could be flexible", names the feeling to herself and waits. Tom says he will need to check with the hiring manager, but that it is within the band. She thanks him.

She also keeps her voice level when she names the figure, without a rising tone at the end, which would have made it sound like a question.

When Tom does reply, she resists the temptation to thank him effusively, which can sound like relief, and simply says that she would appreciate it.

steps.label: Say what matters plainly
steps.text:
When Tom says the start date is fixed, Leila feels a flash of frustration. Instead of letting it into her voice or hiding it entirely, she puts it into words, calmly: "That's hard for me, because I'm committed to finishing a project at my current job, and I'd rather not leave them in the lurch. Is there any room?" Tom says he will ask whether she could join the launch team a little later.

Tom's tone softens noticeably after she explains. It is easier for him to argue her case internally when he knows the reason.

Afterwards, she notices that saying the frustration in words made it fade. Hiding it would have kept it running in the background for the rest of the call.

steps.label: Take time before agreeing
steps.text:
By the end of the call, Tom has agreed in principle to two days' flexibility, a start date four weeks out and a salary three thousand higher, with a review after six months. He asks whether she can accept now. She says that it sounds very good and that she would like to sleep on it and confirm in the morning. She has learned that the moment of greatest pressure is the worst moment to decide.

She also asks Tom to send the revised offer in writing, so that she can check every detail in the morning rather than relying on memory of a phone call.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
In the morning she rereads her priorities, sees that the offer meets the first fully and the other two in part, and accepts. Six months later, at her review, she gets the remaining two thousand. She reflects that the most useful things in the negotiation were her questions, her pause after the number and her request for a night to think, and that none of them depended on reading Tom's body at all.

She also sends Tom a short thank-you note, because she will be working with the company for years, and the negotiation was the first piece of that relationship.

moreFailures.title: Reading restraint as weakness
moreFailures.body:
Negotiators from cultures or backgrounds in which open anger is unusual or inappropriate may stay calm and quiet under pressure. A negotiator who expects displays of feeling may read that calm as a weak position or a lack of commitment, and push harder. Adam, Shirako and Maddux found that anger drew larger concessions from European American negotiators but smaller ones from Asian and Asian American negotiators, and that what mattered was whether anger was seen as appropriate. Pressing with anger on someone who reads it as a breach of decorum is likely to cost you, not them. The same caution applies to silence, formality and indirectness, which mean different things in different places, as the chapter on cultural variance in Part V describes. Before reading a counterpart's restraint, ask what restraint means where they come from.

It also helps to remember that your own calm may be read as weakness by someone who expects displays of feeling. Words can clarify what your face does not show.

moreFailures.title: Choosing the wrong channel for the relationship
moreFailures.body:
Many people choose how to negotiate by convenience: an email because it is quick, a video call because it saves travel. Swaab and colleagues' work suggests that the right channel depends on the relationship. For people who start out neutral, richer channels such as video or a face-to-face meeting tend to help, because faces and voices build trust; a tense exchange of emails between strangers can easily harden. For people who are already hostile, richer channels can make things worse, because there is more to misread and react to, as Harry and Jonny found. Before a negotiation, ask what the relationship is like now. If it is neutral, meet or call. If it is hostile, consider exchanging proposals in writing first and meeting once the gap has narrowed. And whatever the channel, avoid making a final decision in the middle of a heated exchange.

Phone calls sit between the two: voices without faces, which can suit a relationship that is cool but not yet hostile.

moreFailures.title: Filling every silence
moreFailures.body:
Silence in a negotiation is uncomfortable, and the person who has just named a number usually feels it most. Many people fill it, as Omar did, with a concession, a justification or a lower figure, before the other side has said anything at all. They are negotiating against themselves. The other person's silence is rarely a tactic and rarely a refusal. It is usually thinking, writing or simply the time it takes to respond. When you have made your point, stop. Breathe out, keep your face relaxed and let the other person answer. If the silence goes on, ask a question rather than offering a concession. Practise holding a few seconds of quiet in low-stakes conversations, so that it feels ordinary when it matters. A silence is only pressure if you treat it as one.

It also helps to have decided, before the conversation, the figure below which you will not go. Then a silence cannot move you below it.

moreFailures.title: Taking a still face personally
moreFailures.body:
Many professional negotiators keep their faces still at the table, as the chapter on the poker face earlier in this part describes, because composure helps them think and avoids giving away a reaction they have not yet considered. Across the table, a still face is easily read as contempt, hostility or a refusal, and some negotiators respond to that reading by becoming hostile themselves. The exchange then escalates over nothing. If your counterpart's face gives you little, do not fill the gap with the worst interpretation. Treat it as neutral, ask questions and listen to the words. If you need to know how something has landed, ask: "How does that sound from your side?" A still face is usually a person thinking, not a verdict, and the chapter's main point applies: attention beats reading.

If you are the one with the still face, a word of warmth at the start and a "Let me think about that" at the key moments can stop your composure being read as contempt.

And if you are negotiating by video, remember that compression and a small frame make neutral faces look flatter still.

questions.q: Can't experienced negotiators read bluffs from body language?
questions.a:
The evidence suggests not. As the chapter on deception in Part I described, people's accuracy at detecting lies from behaviour is only slightly better than chance, and the cues most often believed to signal lying, such as averted gaze, face-touching and fidgeting, are among the weakest. Experience does not seem to help much, and high stakes may make negotiators more suspicious rather than more accurate. Some people feel confident that they can read a bluff, but confidence and accuracy are poorly linked. The useful skills at the table are different: preparing your priorities and alternatives, asking questions that reveal the other side's interests, listening to the answers and managing your own state. These are reliable in a way that tells are not.

If you want to understand the other side better, the most reliable method is still the oldest: ask, and listen to the answer.

In short: you will learn far more from what people tell you than from what you think their hands are telling you.

questions.q: Is it wrong to mirror the other person's posture?
questions.a:
Natural mimicry is not wrong; it happens on its own when two people are genuinely attending to each other, and it tends to build liking and trust. Maddux and colleagues found that negotiators instructed to mimic their counterparts subtly got better outcomes, through increased trust. But deliberately copying someone's posture in order to make them trust you is manufacturing a signal, and this book does not teach it. It is also fragile: people who notice they are being copied tend to feel manipulated, and trust obtained by technique collapses when it is discovered. The honest route is the one the research points to underneath the technique: real attention to the other person. If you are genuinely listening, your bodies will tend to fall into step without any instruction.

If you find yourself thinking about your posture during a negotiation, turn your attention back to what the other person is saying.

questions.q: What should I do if the other side gets angry?
questions.a:
Slow down, and treat the anger as information about their situation rather than as proof of their limits. Van Kleef and colleagues found that people concede to angry counterparts because they infer that anger means the other side is near walking away, but that is often not true. Ask what has happened, as Bella eventually did: "I can hear you're unhappy about this, can you tell me what's changed?" Listen to the answer before you offer anything. Check your own alternatives, because the effect of anger is strongest on people who feel they have no other options. If the anger becomes abusive, it is fine to pause the conversation and come back to it. Concede only what is warranted by the problem, not what would make the discomfort stop fastest.

And remember that you do not have to answer anger in the moment. "Let me look into this and call you back" is a perfectly good response.

questions.q: Should I show my own frustration in a negotiation?
questions.a:
If you genuinely feel it, put it into words, calmly, rather than performing it or burying it. Côté, Hideg and van Kleef found that faked anger made counterparts demand more, because it reduced their trust, while felt anger expressed honestly could lower demands. Adam and colleagues found that whether anger helps depends heavily on whether the other side sees it as appropriate, which varies by culture and setting. A sentence such as "That's a real problem for my team, because it would mean missing our deadline" tells the other side what matters and why, without escalating. It gives them information they can work with. What tends to backfire is a raised voice, a slammed folder or an act of outrage designed to push them back.

If you are not sure whether anger would be seen as appropriate, plain words about what matters and why are safe almost everywhere.

questions.q: Is it better to negotiate by email, phone or in person?
questions.a:
It depends on the relationship. Swaab and colleagues' combined analysis found that richer channels, video and face to face, led to better outcomes for people who started out neutral towards each other, made little difference for people already inclined to cooperate, and could make outcomes worse for people who were already hostile. For a first negotiation with a supplier or a new employer, a call or a meeting usually helps. For a dispute that has already turned bitter, written proposals may cool things down before you meet. Many negotiations use a mix: a call to build the relationship, written terms to fix the details, and a meeting to close. The research also found the benefit of rich channels weaker in East Asian cultures, so none of this is universal.

Whatever the channel, follow an important conversation with a short written summary, so that both sides agree on what was said.

If you do meet in person, consider the geography too: side by side over a shared document often feels less like a contest than facing each other across a table.

questions.q: How can I stop myself conceding late in a long negotiation?
questions.a:
Plan for tiredness, because it will come. Eat beforehand and keep water nearby. Agree breaks at the start, rather than waiting until someone needs one, and take one before any significant decision rather than after it. Decide in advance which points you will not give up and write them down, so that you can check them when you are tired rather than relying on judgment at the end of the day. Notice the signs that you are depleted: a tight jaw, irritation over small things, a wish to be finished. When you notice them, say that you need a short time to think, or that you would like to sleep on the final terms. Very few good deals are lost by waiting until the morning.

It also helps to bring someone with you in very long negotiations, who can notice when you are flagging and suggest a break.

watch.title: Chris Voss: How to Win Negotiations with Tactical Empathy
watch.notice: A former FBI hostage negotiator on tactical empathy. Listen for how much of his approach depends on voice, pace and naming the other side's feelings.

reviewPrompt: In your next negotiation, ask what the other side needs instead of watching for tells, and take a breath before any concession.
